control_ladder.note_beginner: Strip every fruit off the tree before winter, and pick up the split and dropped ones under it. Leaf-footed bugs spend the winter as adults, and a pomegranate with cracked old fruit left hanging is one of their favorite places to do it, so fruit left on the tree in November is next spring's bugs. Clear the other places they hide too, where they are yours to clear: woodpiles, sheds and outbuildings, and loose bark on nearby eucalyptus, juniper or cypress.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's instruction for pomegranate is to remove all fruit before winter, because orchards with cracked and split fruit left on the trees are a favored overwintering site and large numbers can pass the winter in fruit culls. Adults leave the tree by late November for sheltered aggregations in citrus, juniper, cypress and palms, woodpiles and outbuildings, so a mild winter or a heavy population the previous fall is the signal for a bad year. Cold near 21°F kills some exposed bugs and spares the sheltered ones, which is why harborage matters more than the thermometer.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the weedy patches near the tree mowed or cleared. Through winter and spring, when there is no fruit to feed on, the bugs live on weeds, so a weedy corner next to a pomegranate feeds them until the fruit comes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy areas are the bugs' food source from winter into spring, before fruit is available, and UC IPM's advice is to eliminate such areas near the garden or keep them closely mowed; the Pest Note names thistles and other weeds. This lowers the population that arrives on the young fruit rather than touching anything already on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Head out early, while the morning is still cool and the bugs are sluggish, and brush them off into soapy water or crush them; wear gloves, because they smell when handled. The best time is early in the season, when the newly hatched young sit in tight clusters and you can get a whole batch at once. Scrape off the egg strands on the undersides of leaves as well. On a taller tree, knock the young bugs down with a stick or a hard jet from the hose onto a white sheet spread underneath, then step on them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Hand removal is the primary home control. UC IPM's sequence: morning, to limit movement and flight; as early in the season as possible, while nymphs are still tightly clustered; destroy the egg masses on leaf undersides; a dedicated handheld vacuum works if used regularly. For late-season infestations on pomegranate trees, prune so there is space between the limbs and the ground, then dislodge the nymphs with a stick, by shaking the limbs, or with a pressure nozzle, repeating every 1 to 2 weeks until most are gone. That knock-down does not dislodge eggs and is less effective on adults, which fly; a white ground cover under the tree makes the fallen insects easy to see.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a plant small enough to wrap completely, a light fabric cover keeps the bugs off the fruit. It must be in place before the bugs show up in late spring, or you seal them in with the fruit, and it shuts out the bees and helpful insects along with the pests, so it is a poor fit for a big shrub in full bloom.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM lists row cover as a way to prevent feeding, with two conditions: apply it early, before the bugs arrive and lay eggs, or they are enclosed with the plant, and accept that it also excludes pollinators and beneficial insects. On pomegranate the adults move onto newly developing fruit in late spring to early summer, which overlaps a long, protracted bloom, so this suits a young or container plant far more than a mature tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Tiny native wasps lay their eggs inside the bug's eggs and kill them before they hatch, and assassin bugs, spiders and birds take some of the rest. Give these helpers pollen and nectar flowers to feed on, and skip the broad-acting sprays, which take the helpers down with the bugs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The egg parasite Gryon pennsylvanicum, if not disrupted, can reduce populations by killing eggs before they hatch. Tachinid flies such as Trichopoda pennipes parasitize adults, and assassin bugs, spiders and birds are the named predators. UC IPM's two conditions for keeping them: avoid persistent broad-spectrum insecticides, and provide pollen and nectar sources for the adult beneficials.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Soap spray only works on the very young bugs, and only where it wets them, so its place is a cluster of newly hatched nymphs you can soak directly. It does nothing to the adults, and UC IPM says sprays are rarely needed for this pest, since a few blemishes on home fruit are tolerable.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's ranking for the home grower: insecticidal soap, neem oil and pyrethrin may provide some control of young nymphs only, and most insecticides available to homeowners have only temporary effects on this bug. Since feeding damage on pomegranate is internal and light feeding usually goes unnoticed, a soap spray is a supplement to hand removal at the clustered-nymph stage, not a substitute for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Permethrin and its relatives are the one kind of spray that really knocks this bug down, and UC IPM still says it is rarely worth it: these products are quite toxic to bees and to the helpful insects that were keeping the bugs in check, so the problem can come back worse. If you use one, keep it off anything in flower, and follow the label's waiting time before picking.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Broad-spectrum pyrethroids such as permethrin are the most effective insecticides against leaffooted bug, and the same document notes they are quite toxic to bees and beneficial insects and that insecticides are rarely needed because small blemishes are tolerable in a garden. There is no treatment threshold for this pest on pomegranate, so the decision rests on the previous year's numbers and what you find at fruit set, and the window that matters is ripening from late summer to harvest. Observe the pre-harvest interval on the label.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Often there is no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened and withered. Late-season feeding as the fruit ripens is the worst, and the feeding wounds let opportunistic fungi in to rot the interior.

symptoms_beginner.new: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark and shriveled. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and the holes the bugs make can let rot start inside.

cause_seasoned.new: The leaf-footed bug Leptoglossus zonatus, a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs; gardeners report it most on tomatoes and pomegranates. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed, and their mouthparts carry a yeast, Eremothecium coryli, that discolors the arils; fungal spores follow through the same wound. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations, in woodpiles, outbuildings, under bark and in citrus and juniper, and in cracked pomegranate fruit left on the tree, then disperse when the weather warms and move onto the newly developing fruit in late spring to early summer.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Leptoglossus species' is imprecise where both documents pin the pomegranate pest to L. zonatus; the yeast the documents name and the overwintering sites the sanitation step depends on, including the tree's own leftover fruit, were missing.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: There is no reliable rescue spray for a backyard tree; the controls are physical. Brush or knock adults and nymphs off into soapy water while the morning is still cool, going after the tightly clustered young nymphs early in the season and crushing the egg strands under the leaves. On a taller tree, prune the limbs clear of the ground, then dislodge the nymphs with a stick, by shaking, or with a pressure nozzle every 1 to 2 weeks, with a white sheet beneath to see them. Clear the weedy areas that feed them through winter and spring, strip all fruit before winter, and protect the egg parasites and predators with nectar plants and no broad-spectrum sprays.

The tree knock-down sequence the document gives for pomegranate was missing.

organic_treatment_beginner.new: On a backyard tree the fixes are hands-on. Early in the morning, while it is cool, brush the bugs into soapy water or crush them, starting early in the season when the young are bunched together, and scrape off the egg strands under the leaves. On a tall tree, trim the low limbs off the ground and knock the young bugs down with a stick or a jet of water onto a white sheet, every week or two. Clear weedy patches nearby, take every fruit off before winter, and keep flowers around for the tiny wasps that kill the eggs.

prevention_seasoned.new: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Adults disperse from their winter shelters when the weather warms, in March or April in California's valleys, and enter pomegranate plantings from late spring to feed on the newly developing fruit and reproduce; the aggregations of nymphs and adults form on fruit and foliage from late summer and again in winter shelters. Remove all fruit before winter and clear weeds and nearby harborage, because a mild winter or a heavy fall population is the signal for a bad year, and there is no treatment threshold for this pest.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'watch for the adults congregating in spring' is backwards: both documents put aggregation in fall and winter and dispersal in spring. The winter fruit-removal step and the mild-winter signal were missing.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: uc_ipm PN 74168 'When weather gets warm, typically in March in the San Joaquin Valley and April in the Sacramento Valley, adults disperse to find food sources.' / 'Cold winters kill many adults, and major outbreaks often occur after mild winters.'; uc_ipm ag 'By late November, newly developed adults leave pomegranate and form overwintering aggregations' / 'In late spring to early summer, leaffooted bug enter pomegranate orchards to feed on newly developing fruit and reproduce.' / 'Remove all fruit before winter to decrease the number of overwintering bugs.' / 'There are no treatment thresholds for leaffooted bugs in pomegranates.'

prevention_beginner.new: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. The adults spread out from their winter hiding spots as the weather warms and turn up on the young fruit from late spring; the big clusters come later in the summer. Take every fruit off the tree before winter, keep weeds down, and expect more bugs after a mild winter. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.
prevention_beginner.why: 'look for the adults gathering in spring' is backwards (spring is dispersal; aggregations form in fall and winter); the winter fruit removal was missing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen. Soft, sappy new shoots are what these aphids build up on, and a tree that is healthy but not overfed, with steady water and ordinary nutrition, shrugs off numbers that a stressed or lush one cannot.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Two anchored halves. UC IPM's general aphid guidance: high nitrogen favors aphid reproduction, so never use more than necessary. Its pomegranate page adds the other side: maximize tree health with proper nutrients and irrigation, because aphid numbers increase easily on stressed trees. The target is steady, unstressed growth rather than either starvation or a flush of tips.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Blast the colonies on the growing tips with the hose. On a pomegranate the aphids crowd the ends of the new shoots in spring, and once knocked to the ground most never make it back up; nothing is sprayed, so the ladybugs keep working.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's first physical step for sturdy plants. On pomegranate the colonies sit on the shoot tips from March through June and again in fall, so the targets are the tips and any young fruit they have settled on; a morning blast leaves the leaves time to dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ants farm these aphids for their sugar and chase off the ladybugs and lacewings that would eat them. A band of sticky material on a wrap around the trunk, plus trimming off any branch that touches the ground or a fence, keeps the ants out and hands the tree back to its helpers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's pomegranate guidance is that ants hinder natural enemies, so reducing ant numbers improves the success of biological control; the home Pest Note gives the sticky trunk band as the barrier. The band goes on a collar, not bare bark, and only holds while bridges to the ground are pruned away.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This aphid usually gets handled for free. Ladybugs, lacewing and hover fly larvae, and a tiny wasp that lays its eggs inside the aphids keep it down on most trees, and summer heat knocks the aphids back on its own. Skip broad-acting sprays so the helpers survive.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM rates cotton aphid among the most serious pests of pomegranate orchards and in the same sentence says natural enemies may sufficiently control it. The named agents are the parasite Lysiphlebus testaceipes, several lady beetles (ashy gray, nine-spotted, multicolored Asian, convergent), syrphid and cecidomyiid larvae and lacewings. Natural enemy activity slows in summer heat, but heat also suppresses the aphids, and in fall biological control rises with the aphid numbers; ant control is what lets all of it work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When a colony outruns the helpers, a soap spray soaked directly onto the aphids brings it down without lingering on the tree to harm the good insects. Aim at the packed shoot tips and any young fruit they are clustered on, and go again if they rebuild.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's guidance is to choose products least toxic to natural enemies, insecticidal soaps and oils, which when properly used solve most aphid problems; UGA reports that aphids on pomegranate are routinely controlled with soap in other production regions. Contact only, no residue, so coverage of the tips is what decides it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Neem oil is on the short list UC IPM accepts for organic pomegranate. It smothers what it wets, so cover the shoots well; the best-timed use is on the black eggs on the twigs in winter, before they hatch at the end of March.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's organic list for pomegranate is pyrethrins, azadirachtin, neem oil and a peppermint plus rosemary oil product, with the note that coverage is very important and that treatment of the overwintering eggs gives the best control. Cotton aphid overwinters as black eggs on pomegranate stems that hatch around the end of March, so winter is when to look for them and, if last year was bad, to spray. Keep it off open flowers and out of heat above 90°F.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Dense colonies of small, soft aphids on the shoot tips in spring and again in late summer or fall, often on young fruit as well, with attending ants. Leaf curl and stunted shoots are not typical on pomegranate even when spring numbers are high. The damage that matters comes as fruit ripens in August: honeydew collecting between touching fruit leaves rotten spots on the skin, and sooty mold grows on the honeydew on the fruit surface and is hard to remove. In winter, look for the black eggs on the twigs.

The pomegranate-specific damage (honeydew between touching fruit, sooty mold on the rind near ripening) and the winter egg sign were missing.

symptoms_beginner.new: Groups of tiny soft insects packed on the tips of new shoots in spring and again in late summer, sometimes on young fruit, with ants trailing to and from them. On pomegranate they do not usually curl the leaves. The real trouble comes as the fruit ripens in August, when sticky honeydew trapped between fruit that touch causes rotten spots and a black mold coats the skin. In winter you can spot their tiny black eggs on the twigs.

cause_seasoned.new: The cotton aphid, Aphis gossypii, also called the melon aphid, the one aphid the sources name on this crop. It overwinters as eggs on pomegranate stems, hatches around the end of March onto the shoot tips, peaks in spring, is suppressed by summer heat, and builds again in late summer and fall as aphids move in from weeds, cotton, melons and citrus. Its honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from natural enemies.

Check twigs in winter and early spring for the black overwintering eggs, watch the shoot tips from March into June, and keep ants off the tree so the resident parasites and predators can work.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A hard jet from the hose clears the winged adults out of the canopy. On pomegranate the hose earns its keep twice, because keeping the tree watered and the dust down takes away the hot, dry, dusty conditions that suit whiteflies and work against the wasps that kill them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's first physical step is a strong water stream at the adults. The same document notes that watering reduces hot, dry, dusty conditions, which suit whiteflies and hamper their natural enemies, so the hose does two jobs; dust control has no other step of its own here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Yellow sticky cards hung in the branches show you when the winged adults are on the rise, and they may bring the numbers down somewhat, though they will not clear a bad infestation on their own. Get them up before July, when numbers climb on this crop.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Yellow sticky traps monitor adults and at high levels reduce their numbers. On pomegranate the peak is July and August, so hang them by early summer; they say nothing about the nymphs on the leaf undersides, which are what the parasites work on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off and throw away the leaves that are crusted underneath with the flat, unmoving young. Taking those leaves out can drop the numbers to a level the helpful insects can handle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Taking off the leaves that carry the immobile nymphs and pupae can, per UC IPM, bring numbers down to a level the natural enemies then hold. Before stripping leaves, check them with a hand lens for dark parasitized pupae and empty pupae with round exit holes; those leaves are the parasite's nursery and stay on the tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep ants out of the tree; they guard the whiteflies from the insects that would eat them. A sticky band on a wrap around the trunk, and no branches touching the ground, does it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's instruction is to keep ants out of plants since they protect whiteflies from natural enemies; the ash whitefly's parasite is the control that ant exclusion protects.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Outdoors, tiny parasitic wasps, lacewings and ladybugs usually keep whiteflies under control on their own, and the ash whitefly that is common on pomegranate is already well controlled by a wasp across California. Do not spray if you can see the helpers at work: look for dark or empty pupae under the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The parasite Encarsia inaron is the most effective biological control agent of ash whitefly, which is now under good biological control in California and rarely seen in high numbers; lacewings and lady beetles help but are less reliable. The decision check is a hand lens on the leaf undersides: dark parasitized pupae, empty pupae with round exit holes, and adult parasites mean control is coming in a few weeks. Carbaryl, pyrethroids and foliar imidacloprid are named as particularly disruptive to this.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the leaves are yellowing and sticky and you cannot find any of the helpers, soap spray wetted onto the undersides of the leaves is the least harmful option. It only kills what it touches, so cover the undersides and repeat.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's guidance is products least harmful to natural enemies, insecticidal soaps and oils, combined with the practices above; on pomegranate the commercial page treats only in late summer or early fall when honeydew and sooty mold threaten and parasites are not adequate. Silverleaf whitefly moving in from neighboring cotton or melon fields in July and August is the case where numbers can outrun the parasites.

cause_seasoned.new: Mostly the ash whitefly, Siphoninus phillyreae, with the silverleaf whitefly a problem where pomegranates border cotton or melon fields. Small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and develop rapidly in warm weather, peaking in July and August. Like aphids they leave honeydew, sooty mold grows on it on leaves and fruit, and ants tend them for it.

Spare the natural enemies: carbaryl, pyrethroids and foliar imidacloprid are the insecticides UC IPM names as particularly disruptive to them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with the ants. They collect the mealybugs' honeydew and drive off the tiny wasps and beetles that would clean the colony up, so a tree with an ant trail up the trunk builds up mealybugs that a tree without one never sees. Put a band of sticky material on a paper or fabric wrap around the trunk and cut off any branch that touches the ground or a wall, so the trunk is the only way up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's mealybug guidance for fruit trees leads with managing ants, which are attracted to honeydew and inhibit the activities of natural enemies. The parasites that hold grape mealybug in check on pomegranate are small encyrtid wasps that produce several generations per mealybug generation; they are exactly the enemies ants displace. A trunk band on a collar, with skirt pruning to close the bypasses, is the barrier; it does nothing about the colony already present, which the natural enemies then reduce over the following weeks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off or prune out the cottony clumps you can reach, and cut the suckers off the base of the trunk, since the young ones crowd into that growth in early summer. In winter, strip loose bark from the trunk, which is where the egg masses sit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's Pest Note: if you find an infestation, physically remove the insects by handpicking or prune them out. On pomegranate the second-generation crawlers migrate to leaves and fruit from early June into early July and many can be found in the sucker growth at the base of trees, so removing suckers removes a harborage; the eggs overwinter in cottony masses on the trunk under bark, so loose bark comes off in the dormant season. A forceful spray of water reduces exposed colonies on sturdy plants; it does not reach mealybugs inside the calyx.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Most of the time this pest is handled by tiny wasps that lay their eggs in the mealybugs, turning them into yellow mummies, along with a small brown lady beetle, a gall midge and lacewings. control_ladder.note_beginner: If scale is building year after year, the spray three extension services agree on is horticultural oil on the bare tree in winter, which smothers the scale wintering on the bark; the two Southeast guides give it at 3 percent. control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean-up is the control here, because no spray reaches this fungus once the flower closes over it. Pick up and throw away old fruit on and under the tree, especially the dried, shriveled ones, and cut out dead branches; the fungus lives through the winter in that debris and in the dust that blows onto the flowers. At harvest, shake the tree gently so the infected fruit, which look sound but are lighter, drop to the ground, and cut any doubtful fruit open before you store it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The pathogens overwinter on plant debris in or on the soil and in mummified fruit, with airborne spores carried to flowers or wounded fruit in soil dust, so UC IPM's cultural program is dust control and sanitation, removal of old fruit and dead branches. Because the fruit crown covers the blossom tissue, preharvest sprays are generally ineffective, and Georgia's guide says plainly there is no known method of control; petal fall is the most susceptible stage and the bloom is long and protracted, so even commercial bloom sprays rate least effective. Two harvest-time steps belong with sanitation: gently shaking the tree to drop infected but healthy-appearing fruit, and thorough sorting so diseased fruit is not stored. Expected loss is usually under 1 percent and up to 6 percent in a bad year.

cause_seasoned.new: The fungi Alternaria alternata and A. arborescens infect through the open flower, most readily at petal fall, when rain falls during bloom and early fruit development, then grow silently inside the fruit with no external decay. This is a disease of California's hot, dry pomegranate country in years with wet bloom weather: a Georgia survey did not find it, and Florida's disease survey does not list it. The driver is moisture during bloom, not a humid climate as such.

prevention_seasoned.new: Sanitation and dust control through the year, irrigation that avoids water stress and overwatering so fruit does not crack, and management of the insects and birds that puncture fruit. Wet weather during the long bloom, especially at petal fall, is the infection window, and nothing applied afterward reaches the blossom tissue under the crown. Losses are usually under 1 percent and up to 6 percent; no resistant cultivar is named in any source.

prevention_beginner.new: Keep the ground and the tree clean of old fruit and dead branches, keep dust down, and water steadily so the fruit does not split. Keep fruit-piercing bugs and birds off the fruit. The fungus gets in when rain falls on the open flowers, and nothing you spray afterward can reach it, so a wet bloom season means cutting fruit open before you trust it. Most years it spoils only a few fruit.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear away the old fruit still hanging and the ones lying underneath, along with dead branches and the weeds around the base. The mold's spores wait on that material and blow onto the open flowers, and a fruit infected at bloom carries the mold silently until it is picked and washed or stored. Keeping dust down helps for the same reason.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Botrytis spores reside in or on the soil and on previously infected tissue, weeds and old fruit left on the tree or the orchard floor as mummies, and are spread by wind to senescent flower parts. Good orchard management, dust control and sanitation with removal of old fruit and dead branches, reduces the postharvest incidence of the disease; the extended bloom makes bloom sprays uneconomical and the fruit crown blocks preharvest sprays, so this is the field control. Store sound fruit unwashed and cold, since washing or condensation on the blossom end is what wakes the fungus.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the shrub in sun with space around it so the blossoms dry off fast after rain, fog or dew. This mold gets its start on the fading flower parts, and only when they stay wet for hours, so a plant whose flowers dry by mid-morning gives it far fewer chances over a long bloom.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A generic step from UC IPM's home gray mold guidance rather than its pomegranate page: improve air circulation, because spores germinate only after plants have been continuously wet for 6 or more hours or humidity has stayed above about 90 percent that long, with 70°F to 77°F the favored range. On pomegranate the tissue that matters is the senescent flower parts during a long bloom, so the benefit is a shorter wet period on the blossoms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water the ground, not the plant. Irrigation water landing on the open flowers is one of the ways the mold gets its start, along with rain, fog and dew, and you control only the first.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spores on senescent flower tissue such as stamens germinate and infect when there is free water on the surface from rain, dew, fog or irrigation; keeping irrigation off the canopy through bloom removes the one wetting source in your hands. UC IPM's home guidance is drip or microsprinklers rather than wetting foliage. It changes nothing for a fruit already carrying a quiescent infection.

symptoms_seasoned.new: A fuzzy gray coat of spores at the crown (blossom) end, on the old flower parts, appearing after the fruit is washed or held in humid storage rather than on the tree; the crown tissue is colonized and the rot grows into the fruit. Stored fruit at high humidity often decays completely, sometimes with grayish-white mycelium and small black sclerotia on the surface. Decay can also start from the stem-end wound, especially where the stem was torn off entirely.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'spreads in cool, wet, or humid conditions' is wrong on temperature (decay develops quickly at 65 to 75°F) and 'can move between touching fruit' has no anchor on this crop. The record missed that the symptoms appear after harvest, at the blossom end, and from the stem-end wound.

symptoms_beginner.new: A fuzzy gray mold that shows up in the crown end of the fruit, on the dried flower bits, usually after the fruit has been washed or kept somewhere damp, and then spreads into the fruit. In storage a fruit can rot right through, sometimes with grayish-white fuzz and tiny black specks on the skin. Rot can also start where the stem was torn off.

cause_seasoned.new: The fungus Botrytis cinerea infects the flower parts at bloom, when free water from rain, dew, fog or irrigation sits on the senescent stamens, and then stays quiescent inside the crown until the fruit ripens. Washing or condensation on the blossom end activates it, and decay develops quickly at about 65 to 75°F. Spores come from soil, infected debris, weeds and mummified fruit and spread on the wind. It is one of the most important causes of postharvest decay in pomegranates.
cause_seasoned.why: 'cool, wet, humid conditions' and 'overripe fruit' are unanchored: UC IPM gives moderate decay temperatures (65 to 75°F) and a bloom-time infection that stays latent, not an infection of ripe fruit. The latent-infection mechanism, which is why no later spray works, was missing.

cause_beginner.new: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that gets into the flowers during bloom when they are wet from rain, dew, fog or sprinklers, then sits quietly inside the crown of the fruit until picking. Washing the fruit or storing it somewhere damp wakes it up, and it rots fastest at mild room temperatures, around 65 to 75°F. Its spores come from old fruit, weeds and plant litter under the tree. It is a leading cause of rot in stored pomegranates.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: No home spray reaches it: the extended bloom makes bloom sprays impractical and the fruit crown covers the blossom tissue, which is why commercial control is postharvest. At home the controls are sanitation (old fruit, dead branches, weeds) and dust control in the field, then handling: clip the stem rather than pull it, do not wash fruit before storage, and refrigerate promptly at about 41°F with high humidity, since free water and mild temperatures are what activate the fungus. Discard any fruit showing gray fuzz at the crown; it cannot be saved.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'harvest before rains' and 'remove moldy flowers' have no anchor on this crop; the one storage rule the source gives, that washing and condensation activate the fungus, was missing, and the storage temperature was unstated.

organic_treatment_beginner.new: There is no spray that fixes this at home, because the fungus is already sealed under the crown of the fruit before you could reach it. What works: keep old fruit, dead wood and weeds cleared from around the tree, cut the fruit off with a bit of stem instead of pulling it, do not wash fruit you plan to keep, and get it into the refrigerator soon, at about 41°F, since dampness and warmth are what set the mold off. Throw out any fruit with gray fuzz in the crown.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: 'pick before the rains' and 'pick off moldy flowers' have no anchor on this crop; the no-wash storage rule and temperature were missing.

prevention_seasoned.new: Sanitation and dust control in the field, irrigation kept off the flowers through the long bloom, and post-harvest handling: an intact clipped stem, no washing before storage, and quick cooling to about 41°F at high humidity. Air movement around the plant shortens the wet periods on flower tissue that infection needs. Split or wounded fruit is an entry point for other fruit rots; for gray mold the stated wound is the stem end.

At picking, clip the stem instead of tearing it, do not wash fruit you are storing, and chill it soon. Give the plant sun and air so the flowers dry fast after rain or dew.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clean-up is the control. Gather up and dispose of fallen leaves, dropped fruit and dead or spotted stems, and do it thoroughly in winter after the leaves fall, because the fungus waits in that litter for the next season. Prune in winter, when the plant is bare and the fungus is not making spores, and burn or bin what you cut. In South Carolina the spots are common in humid weather and the extension service says they do not need treating; in Florida a neglected planting can lose most of its crop to its fungal diseases together, so the cleanup matters more the wetter your climate.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UF/IFAS puts field sanitation at the center of pomegranate disease management: clear leaf litter, fruit and diseased stems, especially in winter when the trees drop leaves that may be harboring pathogens from the previous season, and remove infected material to a safe distance and burn it as permitted. Prune in winter when spore production is low, or late fall when wounds heal fastest, in dry weather and with angled cuts. Fungicides currently labelled for pomegranate are ineffective against this pathogen per the same document, so there is no spray step; Clemson's home verdict is that the leaf and fruit spots common in humid South Carolina do not require treatment, while UF/IFAS attributes losses of up to 90 percent, from Florida's pomegranate diseases together rather than this fungus alone, to a poorly managed orchard. Resistant varieties are under evaluation at UF, but none is named.

symptoms_seasoned.new: On leaves, small irregular dark brown spots that enlarge, develop a dark brown margin around a gray center, sometimes with concentric rings, and take on a greenish halo as the leaf yellows; severe defoliation follows and can cut yield. On fruit, small irregular black spots that merge into larger blotches, confined to the skin surface; the rind and arils beneath are unaffected, which separates it from anthracnose. Symptoms vary among cultivars. Most common in warm, humid, rainy regions.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'heavily spotted fruit is russeted' has no anchor: UF/IFAS describes superficial black lesions that coalesce into blotches. The leaf lesion description that distinguishes this disease was missing.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: uf_ifas_edis PP349 https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP349 'On the leaves, the symptoms start as small (0.1–0.3 cm), irregularly shaped dark brown lesions. These lesions can expand (0.5–1.2 cm) and develop a distinct, dark brown margin with gray coloration. Sometimes the lesions are large enough to observe concentric rings of alternating dark and light gray in the lesion center. A greenish halo often forms around the lesions and becomes very pronounced as the leaves yellow from chlorosis. Eventually leaves senesce, leading to severe defoliation, which can reduce yields. Symptoms on the fruit are small irregular black lesions that can later coalesce into bigger blotches. Lesions caused by P. punicae on the fruits are superficial only, contrary to Colletotrichum and other fungal pathogens, which affect the rind and arils. The symptoms on leaves and fruits can vary among the different pomegranate varieties.' (read first-party 2026-09-04)

symptoms_beginner.new: Small dark brown spots on the leaves that grow, turn gray in the middle with a dark rim, and get a greenish ring around them as the leaf yellows; a badly hit plant drops most of its leaves. On the fruit, small black spots that run together into blotches on the skin only, without rotting the inside. It is worst in warm, humid, rainy areas.

cause_seasoned.new: The fungus Pseudocercospora punicae (Cercospora punicae in older references), a very common disease of pomegranate in Florida and found on harvested fruit in Georgia. It is one organism; anthracnose (Colletotrichum) and Botryosphaeria stem canker are separate diseases that often occur alongside it in the same humid climates. The fungus carries over in leaf litter, dropped fruit and diseased stems from the previous season, and humid subtropical weather favors it.

'thrives on prolonged leaf and fruit wetness' is stated for anthracnose, not this fungus, and 'a leading reason pomegranate fruits poorly in the Southeast' is no source's claim.

It is one disease; the anthracnose and stem canker fungi that show up in the same humid places are different problems. It survives from one year to the next in fallen leaves, old fruit and diseased stems, and damp, warm weather favors it.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Sanitation is the control: clear leaf litter, dropped fruit and diseased stems, above all in winter after leaf fall, and remove or burn infected material. Prune in winter when spore production is low, in dry weather, with angled cuts. UF/IFAS states that fungicides currently labelled for pomegranate are ineffective against this pathogen, and Clemson's home verdict is that the leaf and fruit spots common in humid South Carolina do not require treatment. Losses of up to 90 percent, to Florida's fungal diseases together rather than this one alone, are reported only for a poorly managed orchard, so the cleanup is what separates a nuisance from a loss.

Gather up fallen leaves, dropped fruit and spotted or dead stems, especially in winter after the leaves come down, and prune in winter when the plant is bare. Florida's specialists say the fungicides sold for pomegranate do not work on this fungus, and South Carolina's say the spots do not need treating. A plant that is kept clean gets a few spots; a neglected one in a wet climate can lose most of its fruit to this and the other fungal diseases together.
